title: The December Payment Freeze: Why Your Best Corporate Clients Go Quiet for Six Weeks
linkedin:
November usually ends on a high note. Invoices are out, the pipeline is full, and the sales number for the month looks genuinely strong.

Here's the part that catches a lot of owner-led businesses every single year: some of your biggest clients are about to stop paying you, not because anything is wrong, but because their accounts payable team is about to go on leave.

Large corporate customers, government departments and franchise head offices typically run their final payment cycle of the year in the first half of December, then don't process another run until late January. Work delivered and invoiced now can sit unpaid for six to eight weeks, purely because there's nobody left at their end to approve it.

None of that shows up as a profit problem. It shows up as an overdraft you didn't plan for, a supplier payment you delay, or a short-term top-up you ask a director for, right when wages, rent and the 28 January superannuation guarantee are all still due on schedule.

The fix isn't a harder conversation in December. It's one simple question, asked now: what date does each major client's payment run actually close for the year, and when does the first one in January land. Once that date is known, invoicing can be brought forward to clear it, instead of drifting past it into the gap by accident.

The businesses that feel this hardest are usually the ones with one or two large clients making up most of the debtor book. Worth mapping now, while there's still a week or two to act on it.

Full piece on the ProfitPulse blog.
